overview: Phrygian communities built an influential Iron Age kingdom in Anatolia, with Gordion as its principal royal centre. Their monumental buildings, workshops and burials preserve evidence of power and daily work. The map’s broad 1500-500 BCE span is not the documented lifetime of that kingdom: its start is much too early, and the same large outline cannot show changing political control. This card focuses on the better-attested Iron Age society and its later continuity.

periods.title: A monumental royal centre
periods.summary: During the tenth and ninth centuries BCE, Gordion developed substantial fortifications and elite buildings.

periods.title: The era of Midas and regional influence
periods.summary: Phrygian power reached its greatest prominence under Midas in the late eighth century BCE.

periods.title: Lydian and Persian dominance
periods.summary: Lydian rule was followed by incorporation into the Persian Empire during the sixth century BCE. The population and settlement continued.

items.text: The historical Midas appears as Mita in late-eighth-century Assyrian records. He was a significant opponent of Assyrian ambitions in Anatolia. The later tale that everything he touched became gold is a myth; excavated palaces and the diplomatic record provide firmer evidence for his kingdom’s wealth and influence.

Gordion’s monumental gateway still has stone walls standing about ten metres high. A visitor approaching it would have encountered a carefully built statement of royal strength. Behind the defences stood large halls, workshops and the institutions needed to sustain a major Iron Age centre.

Elite buildings at Gordion contained early coloured pebble mosaics, with stones arranged into lively geometric patterns. The builders also tackled long timber roof spans. These achievements depended on planning and skilled construction, extending royal display from the city’s massive entrance to the floor under a visitor’s feet.

In the Terrace Building and nearby workshops, cooking areas stood beside rooms with grinding platforms and textile tools. Workers turned grain into flour while others prepared thread and cloth. The repeated layouts point to organized production on a substantial scale, although the tools alone cannot identify each worker’s social status.

Archaeologists inventoried more than a thousand spindle whorls at Gordion. These small clay weights helped spinners make thread. Other clay weights kept hanging threads taut on upright looms. Some of the city’s grandest economic achievements depended on very small objects doing their jobs over and over.

Outside the citadel, excavated homes had hearths, ovens, grinding benches and plastered storage bins. Some rooms had stone paving and mud-brick walls strengthened with wooden posts. Preparing food and making textiles were part of life here too, beyond the monumental spaces associated with rulers.

Wooden objects from Gordion’s elite tombs include tables, stools, bowls and spoons, as well as elaborately decorated furniture. Dry, relatively stable tomb interiors helped them survive. Craftspeople chose woods such as boxwood, juniper and walnut, combining different materials with carving, inlay and bronze decoration.

Wooden plates from Tumulus W preserve early, securely dated evidence for lathe work. Turning wood allowed craftspeople to shape a piece as it rotated. Careful study of tool marks can recover a workshop technique even when the workshop and its tools have disappeared.

sections.title: A child’s small chariot and a very large meal

items.text: The rich child burial called Tumulus P contained a small toy quadriga, a four-horse chariot. This is a glimpse of an object placed with one privileged child, not a catalogue of every child’s playthings. Its miniature horse equipment became the subject of detailed archaeological study.

Most people did not receive a vast burial mound. In Gordion’s Common Cemetery, excavators catalogued 112 graves, and only 34 contained even modest offerings. Comparing these burials with lavish tumuli reveals differences in wealth and funerary treatment that the royal monuments alone would hide.

Residues in vessels from Tumulus MM suggest a funeral meal of meat and legumes, with a fermented drink combining grape wine, barley beer and honey. The proposed menu comes from chemical analysis. It describes an exceptional royal occasion, rather than what every Phrygian family ate for dinner.

The funeral equipment included three large cauldrons, each capable of holding about 150 litres, and animal-headed pouring vessels. Serving tables and drinking bowls helped researchers reconstruct how the mourners were supplied. This was a meal requiring serious organization, not simply one oversized cup.

The man in Tumulus MM lay in a log coffin on dyed textiles. The excavators observed purple and brown traces when the chamber was opened. Furniture and fabrics accompanied the burial, preserving evidence of care, ceremony and costly craftsmanship even where organic materials normally decay.

sections.title: Names in stone, dates in wood

items.text: At the rock-cut Midas Monument near Yazılıkaya, the Phrygian inscription includes “midai lavagtaei”, meaning “for Midas the leader”. This is a modern Latin-letter transcription of the ancient alphabet. The sixth-century BCE monument is later than the famous eighth-century king; which Midas it invokes remains a historical question.

The same monument belongs to the worship of Matar, the Phrygian Mother Goddess. Its façade and niche connected a divine presence with the named people who commissioned work. A dedication could preserve a patron’s ambitions alongside a community’s religious setting.

Tree-ring research moved Tumulus MM’s construction to around 740 BCE. Since Assyrian records still place Midas in power in 709 BCE, its occupant cannot readily be the famous king himself. The label “Midas Mound” survived a major change in what archaeologists think the tomb represents.

Excavations began with the Körte brothers in 1900 and expanded under Rodney Young from 1950. Investigators uncovered citadels, tombs and earlier settlement layers. Separating those layers matters: people lived at Gordion before the Phrygian kingdom, and continued using the site after its independence ended.

Phrygian writing continued far beyond the map’s 500 BCE cutoff. In Roman-period funerary inscriptions, Greek might record a dead person’s details while Phrygian supplied a warning against disturbing the grave. These later bilingual texts show a continuing language in a changed political and social world.

ending.text: The independent kingdom gave way to Lydian dominance and then Persian rule in the sixth century BCE. Gordion remained an important district centre. Phrygian communities and their language continued under later powers, so neither a single destruction layer nor the map’s 500 BCE endpoint marks the disappearance of the people.
